newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan seeks solace in party applause.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan seeks solace in party applause.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, his rule challenged over a bungled trip to Libya, heads for a party congress at the weekend hoping to forget his worst week in power in a dazzle of pyrotechnics and chanting crowds.
The pro-Islamic Welfare Party plans to gather 10,000 flag-waving supporters to greet leader Erbakan at Sunday's conference, its first in two years.
A giant poster of the white-haired prime minister will adorn a sports hall where he is guaranteed to be re-elected as party head. Erbakan, 69, is the sole candidate.
"It will be the first congress we have had in government and that's why we're trying to make it stunning," conference organiser and Welfare MP Seref Malkoc told Reuters.
But Erbakan will soon come down to earth under opposition attempts next week to topple him after only three months as modern Turkey's first Islamist leader.

He stands accused of bringing Turkey into disrepute for visiting outcast state Libya last week and giving its leader Muammar Gaddafi a platform to roundly criticise Turkey's treatment of its Kurds and close ties to the West.
Turkey's NATO ally the United States has harshly rebuked Erbakan for lending Gaddafi verbal support against Washington.
The main opposition Motherland Party (ANAP) on Friday predicted that MPs from Welfare's pro-Western coalition allies would rebel at a censure motion next Wednesday against Erbakan.
"We expect MPs to break party discipline and take the censure motion on board," senior ANAP member Murat Basesgioglu told a news conference.
Erbakan, who would have to resign if he lost the vote, was confident on Friday. "The censure motion will strengthen us," Anatolian news agency quoted him as saying at a party meeting.
"They are not even worth wasting breath on," he said in reference to talks between divided secularist MPs on forming a anti-Welfare government without going to fresh elections.
On paper, he has the backing of 281 MPs, five more than is needed to win the vote, but some members of partner Tansu Ciller's True Path Party (DYP) are uneasy with the Libya affair.

However, analysts say the vast majority of DYP MPs are likely to stick with Erbakan for fear of a return of the political chaos that deprived Turkey of steady leadership for nine months before Welfare entered government in June.

Erbakan has so far failed in promises to solve a 12-year-old Kurdish rebel campaign through "Moslem brotherhood". Populist measures, like 50 percent wage rises for more than seven million civil servants, have burdened the shaky economy.
Turkey's top banker rang alarm bells on the economy on Friday, predicting a sharp increase in deficits this year.

However, gloomy scenarios will be far from Erbakan's mind on Sunday -- at least temporarily. Congress organisers promise a spectacular show, including laser displays, fireworks and use of the latest video techniques.
Welfare, the most disciplined party in Turkey, looks to be firmly behind Erbakan after he snuffed out a leadership challenge to a provincial party boss close to him last month.
Supporters will only be allowed to chant slogans authorised by party officials to prevent the congress turning into a radical Islamist gathering that would disturb Turkey's secularist majority.
